title: Design Kafka — Producers & Consumers
description: Deep dive into Kafka producer batching and compression, acks modes, consumer group rebalancing, and offset commit strategies that determine your delivery guarantees.

segments.text: The Kafka producer seems simple — send a message to a topic. But the producer's configuration determines your throughput, latency, and durability guarantees. LinkedIn's Kafka producers handle over seven trillion messages per day. Every producer setting is a tradeoff between these three dimensions.

Producers batch messages before sending. The batch.size parameter controls the maximum batch size in bytes — default sixteen kilobytes. The linger.ms parameter adds a delay to accumulate more messages — default zero. Set linger to five milliseconds and batch size to sixty-four kilobytes, and throughput can jump ten times while adding minimal latency.

Compression happens at the batch level, not individual messages. This is genius — compressing a batch of similar messages gets much better ratios than individual compression. LZ4 gives the best speed-to-ratio balance. Snappy is slightly faster. ZSTD gives the best compression ratio. LinkedIn uses LZ4 and sees four to five times compression on JSON messages.

The acks setting is the most critical producer config. Acks equals zero: fire and forget, maximum throughput, data loss possible. Acks equals one: leader acknowledges, fast but data loss if leader crashes before replication. Acks equals all: all in-sync replicas must acknowledge. Use acks-all for anything you can't afford to lose.

Consumer groups enable parallel processing. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group. Ten partitions and five consumers means each consumer handles two partitions. Add a sixth consumer and one partition rebalances to it. Add an eleventh consumer and one sits idle — you can never have more consumers than partitions.

Consumer group rebalancing is the most painful Kafka operation. When a consumer joins or leaves, all partitions are reassigned. During rebalancing, no consumer processes any messages — this is a full stop-the-world event. Cooperative rebalancing in newer Kafka versions only reassigns affected partitions, reducing the disruption window.

Your consumer is processing a message that takes thirty seconds — a complex ML inference. The consumer group coordinator thinks the consumer is dead because it hasn't sent a heartbeat. It triggers a rebalance. How do you prevent this?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you handle long-running message processing without triggering false rebalances?

segments.text: Offset commit strategies determine your delivery guarantee. Auto-commit: offsets committed every five seconds automatically. If the consumer crashes between commits, messages are reprocessed — at-least-once. Manual commit after processing: also at-least-once but more controlled. Commit before processing: at-most-once, messages can be lost.

Consumer back-pressure is often overlooked. If your consumer can't keep up with the producer rate, lag grows unboundedly. Monitor consumer lag as a key metric. Set alerts when lag exceeds a threshold — say one million messages. Options: add more consumers, increase partition count, or accept eventual processing at the current rate.

You're designing a Kafka-based order processing system. Orders must never be lost, must be processed in order per customer, and the system handles fifty thousand orders per second. What are your producer and consumer configurations?
segments.thought_prompt: Design Kafka producer/consumer config for 50K orders/sec with no-loss and per-customer ordering.

segments.text: Kafka producers and consumers are tuning machines. Batch and compress for throughput, use acks-all for durability, partition by business key for ordering, use cooperative rebalancing for stability, and commit offsets manually for control. Next lesson, we'll tackle the replication layer that makes all of this durable.
